title: Chapter 1 — Exterior Form Of North America
paragraphs: North America presents in its external form certain general features that are easy to discern at first glance. A kind of methodical order seems to have governed the separation of land and water, mountains and valleys. A simple but grand arrangement can be seen amid the confusion of objects and the prodigious variety of scenes. This continent is divided, almost equally, into two vast regions. One is bounded on the north by the Arctic Pole and on the east and west by the two great oceans; it stretches southward, forming a triangle whose irregular sides eventually meet below the great lakes of Canada. The second region begins where the first ends and takes in all the rest of the continent. The one slopes gently toward the Pole, the other toward the Equator.

The territory covered by the first region descends toward the north with a slope so imperceptible that it may almost be said to form a level plain. Within the bounds of this immense stretch of country there are neither high mountains nor deep valleys. Streams meander through it irregularly; great rivers mingle their currents, separate and meet again, scatter and form vast marshes, losing all trace of their channels in the labyrinth of waters they themselves have created. Then at length, after innumerable windings, they fall into the Polar Seas. The great lakes that bound this first region are not walled in, like most of those in the Old World, between hills and rocks. Their banks are flat and rise only a few feet above the level of their waters. Each of them thus forms a vast bowl filled to the brim. The slightest change in the structure of the globe would send their waters rushing either toward the Pole or to the tropical sea.

The second region is more varied on its surface and better suited for human habitation. Two long chains of mountains divide it from one end to the other: the Alleghany ridge follows the shape of the Atlantic shore, and the other runs parallel with the Pacific. The space lying between these two chains of mountains contains 1,341,649 square miles. *a Its surface is therefore about six times as great as that of France. This vast territory, however, forms a single valley. One side descends gradually from the rounded summits of the Alleghanies, while the other rises in an uninterrupted course toward the tops of the Rocky Mountains. At the bottom of the valley flows an immense river, into which the various streams issuing from the mountains fall from all sides. In memory of their native land, the French once called this river the St. Louis. The Indians, in their pompous language, have named it the Father of Waters, or the Mississippi.
a [ Darby's "View of the United States."]

The Mississippi takes its source above the line between the two great regions I have spoken of, not far from the highest point of the table-land where they meet. Near the same spot rises another river, *b which empties into the Polar seas. The course of the Mississippi is at first uncertain: it winds several times toward the north, from which it rose, and at length, after being delayed in lakes and marshes, it flows slowly onward to the south. Sometimes gliding quietly along the clay bed nature has assigned to it, sometimes swollen by storms, the Mississippi waters 2,500 miles in its course. *c At a distance of 1,364 miles from its mouth, this river reaches an average depth of fifteen feet, and it is navigated by vessels of 300 tons burden for nearly 500 miles. Fifty-seven large navigable rivers contribute to swell its waters: among others, the Missouri, which covers 2,500 miles; the Arkansas, 1,300 miles; the Red River, 1,000 miles; four whose course runs from 800 to 1,000 miles, namely, the Illinois, the St. Peter's, the St. Francis, and the Moingona; and a countless multitude of smaller streams that unite their tributary waters from every side.
c [ Warden's "Description of the United States."]

The valley watered by the Mississippi seems formed to be the bed of this mighty river, which, like a god of antiquity, dispenses both good and evil along its course. On the banks of the stream nature displays an inexhaustible fertility; but as you move away from its banks, vegetation grows weaker, the soil becomes poor, and the plants that survive grow sickly. Nowhere have the great convulsions of the globe left more evident traces than in the valley of the Mississippi; the whole aspect of the country shows the powerful effects of water, both in its fertility and in its barrenness. The waters of the primeval ocean piled up enormous beds of vegetable soil in the valley, which they leveled as they retreated. On the right bank of the river one sees immense plains, as smooth as if a farmer had passed over them with his roller. As you approach the mountains, the soil becomes more and more uneven and sterile; the ground is pierced, as it were, in a thousand places by primitive rocks that stand out like the bones of a skeleton whose flesh is partly consumed. The surface of the earth is covered with granite sand and huge irregular masses of stone, among which a few plants force their growth, giving the appearance of a green field scattered with the ruins of a vast building. On examination, these stones and this sand show a perfect resemblance to those that form the arid and broken summits of the Rocky Mountains. The flood of waters that washed the soil down to the bottom of the valley afterwards carried off portions of the rocks themselves; and these, dashed and bruised against the neighboring cliffs, were left scattered like wrecks at their feet. *d The valley of the Mississippi is, on the whole, the most magnificent dwelling-place prepared by God for man's abode; and yet at present it may be called a mighty desert.
d [ See Appendix, A.]

On the eastern side of the Alleghanies, between the base of these mountains and the Atlantic Ocean, there lies a long ridge of rocks and sand that the sea appears to have left behind as it retreated. The mean breadth of this territory does not exceed one hundred miles, but it runs about nine hundred miles in length. This part of the American continent has a soil that offers every obstacle to the farmer, and its vegetation is scanty and monotonous.

It was on this inhospitable coast that the first united efforts of human industry were made. That narrow strip of arid land was the cradle of the English colonies that were destined one day to become the United States of America. The center of power still lies here, while in the backwoods the true elements of the great people to whom the future control of the continent belongs are gathering, almost in secret.

When the Europeans first landed on the shores of the West Indies, and afterwards on the coast of South America, they thought themselves transported into those fabled regions of which poets had sung. The sea sparkled with phosphorescent light, and the extraordinary clarity of its waters revealed to the navigator's eye all that had until then been hidden in the deep abyss. *e Here and there appeared little islands perfumed with fragrant plants, looking like baskets of flowers floating on the tranquil surface of the ocean. Every object that met the sight in this enchanting region seemed prepared to satisfy man's wants or contribute to his pleasures. Nearly all the trees were loaded with nourishing fruits, and those that were useless as food delighted the eye with the brilliance and variety of their colors. In groves of fragrant lemon trees, wild figs, flowering myrtles, acacias, and oleanders, hung with festoons of climbing plants covered in flowers, a multitude of birds unknown in Europe displayed their bright plumage, glittering with purple and azure, and mingled their song with the harmony of a world teeming with life and motion. *f Beneath this brilliant exterior, death lay concealed. But the air of these climates had so enervating an influence that man, absorbed in present enjoyment, became heedless of the future.

e [ Malte Brun tells us (vol. v. p. 726) that the water of the Caribbean Sea is so transparent that corals and fish are discernible at a depth of sixty fathoms. The ship seemed to float in air, the navigator became giddy as his eye penetrated through the crystal flood, and beheld submarine gardens, or beds of shells, or gilded fishes gliding among tufts and thickets of seaweed.]
f [ See Appendix, B.]

North America appeared under a very different aspect; there everything was grave, serious, and solemn. It seemed created to be the domain of the intellect, as the South was that of sensual delight. A turbulent and foggy ocean washed its shores. It was girded by a belt of granite rocks, or by wide tracts of sand. The foliage of its woods was dark and gloomy, for they were made up of firs, larches, evergreen oaks, wild olive trees, and laurels. Beyond this outer belt lay the thick shade of the central forest, where the largest trees produced in the two hemispheres grow side by side. The plane, the catalpa, the sugar maple, and the Virginian poplar mingled their branches with those of the oak, the beech, and the lime. In these, as in the forests of the Old World, destruction was perpetually at work. The ruins of vegetation were heaped on one another, but there was no laboring hand to remove them, and their decay was not rapid enough to make room for the continual work of renewal. Climbing plants, grasses, and other herbs forced their way through the mass of dying trees; they crept along their bending trunks, found nourishment in their dusty hollows, and made a passage beneath the lifeless bark. Thus decay lent its aid to life, and their respective products were mingled together. The depths of these forests were gloomy and obscure, and a thousand small streams, undirected by human industry, kept them constantly moist. It was rare to meet with flowers, wild fruits, or birds beneath their shades. The fall of a tree overthrown by age, the rush of a waterfall, the lowing of the buffalo, and the howling of the wind were the only sounds that broke the silence of nature.

East of the great river, the woods almost disappeared; in their place were seen prairies of immense extent. Whether Nature in her infinite variety had denied the seeds of trees to these fertile plains, or whether they had once been covered with forests later destroyed by the hand of man, is a question that neither tradition nor scientific research has been able to resolve.

These immense deserts were not, however, empty of human inhabitants. Some wandering tribes had for ages been scattered among the forest shades and the green pastures of the prairie. From the mouth of the St. Lawrence to the delta of the Mississippi, and from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean, these savages shared certain points of resemblance that testified to a common origin; yet at the same time they differed from all other known races of men: *g they were neither white like the Europeans, nor yellow like most of the Asiatics, nor black like the negroes. Their skin was reddish brown, their hair long and shining, their lips thin, and their cheekbones very prominent. The languages spoken by the North American tribes varied greatly in their words, but were subject to the same grammatical rules. These rules differed in several respects from those observed to govern the origin of language elsewhere. The idiom of the Americans seemed the product of new combinations, and bespoke an effort of understanding of which the Indians of our day would be incapable. *h

g [ With the progress of discovery some resemblance has been found to exist between the physical conformation, the language, and the habits of the Indians of North America, and those of the Tongous, Mantchous, Mongols, Tartars, and other wandering tribes of Asia. The land occupied by these tribes is not very distant from Behring's Strait, which allows of the supposition, that at a remote period they gave inhabitants to the desert continent of America. But this is a point which has not yet been clearly elucidated by science. See Malte Brun, vol. v.; the works of Humboldt; Fischer, "Conjecture sur l'Origine des Americains"; Adair, "History of the American Indians."]
h [ See Appendix, C.]

The social state of these tribes also differed in many respects from all that was seen in the Old World. They seemed to have multiplied freely in the midst of their deserts without coming into contact with other races more civilized than their own. Accordingly, they showed none of those vague, incoherent notions of right and wrong, none of that deep corruption of manners that is usually joined with ignorance and coarseness among nations which, after advancing to civilization, have relapsed into a state of barbarism. The Indian was indebted to no one but himself; his virtues, his vices, and his prejudices were his own work; he had grown up in the wild independence of his nature.

If, in polished countries, the lowest of the people are rude and uncivil, it is not merely because they are poor and ignorant, but because, being so, they are in daily contact with rich and enlightened men. The sight of their own hard lot and of their weakness, daily contrasted with the happiness and power of some of their fellow creatures, stirs in their hearts both anger and fear: the consciousness of their inferiority and dependence irritates even as it humiliates them. This state of mind shows itself in their manners and language; they are at once insolent and servile. The truth of this is easily proved by observation: the common people are ruder in aristocratic countries than elsewhere, and in opulent cities than in rural districts. In those places where the rich and powerful gather together, the weak and the poor feel oppressed by their inferior condition. Unable to see a single chance of regaining their equality, they give themselves up to despair and allow themselves to fall below the dignity of human nature.

This unfortunate effect of the disparity of conditions is not to be seen in savage life: the Indians, although ignorant and poor, are equal and free. When Europeans first came among them, the natives of North America had no notion of the value of riches, and were indifferent to the pleasures that civilized man secures for himself through them. Nevertheless there was nothing coarse in their bearing; they practiced a habitual reserve and a kind of aristocratic politeness. Mild and hospitable in peace, though merciless in war beyond any known degree of human ferocity, the Indian would risk dying of hunger to aid the stranger who asked admittance by night at the door of his hut; yet he could tear with his hands the still-quivering limbs of his prisoner. The famous republics of antiquity never gave examples of more unshakable courage, prouder spirits, or more unyielding love of independence than were once hidden among the wild forests of the New World. *i The Europeans made no great impression when they landed on the shores of North America; their presence aroused neither envy nor fear. What influence could they possess over such men as we have described? The Indian could live without wants, suffer without complaint, and pour out his death-song at the stake. *j Like all other members of the great human family, these savages believed in the existence of a better world, and worshiped, under different names, God, the creator of the universe. Their ideas on the great intellectual truths were in general simple and philosophical. *k

i [ We learn from President Jefferson's "Notes upon Virginia," p. 148, that among the Iroquois, when attacked by a superior force, aged men refused to fly or to survive the destruction of their country; and they braved death like the ancient Romans when their capital was sacked by the Gauls. Further on, p. 150, he tells us that there is no example of an Indian who, having fallen into the hands of his enemies, begged for his life; on the contrary, the captive sought to obtain death at the hands of his conquerors by the use of insult and provocation.]

j [ See "Histoire de la Louisiane," by Lepage Dupratz; Charlevoix, "Histoire de la Nouvelle France"; "Lettres du Rev. G. Hecwelder;" "Transactions of the American Philosophical Society," v. I; Jefferson's "Notes on Virginia," pp. 135-190. What is said by Jefferson is of especial weight, on account of the personal merit of the writer, of his peculiar position, and of the matter-of-fact age in which he lived.]
k [ See Appendix, D.]
Although we have here traced the character of a primitive people, there can be no doubt that another people, more civilized and more advanced in every respect, had preceded it in the same regions.

An obscure tradition that prevailed among the Indians north of the Atlantic tells us that these very tribes once dwelt on the west side of the Mississippi. Along the banks of the Ohio, and throughout the central valley, there are still found today tumuli raised by human hands. On exploring these heaps of earth to their center, one commonly finds human bones, strange instruments, arms, and utensils of all kinds, made of metal or intended for purposes unknown to the present race. The Indians of our time can give no information about the history of this unknown people. Nor did those who lived three hundred years ago, when America was first discovered, leave any accounts from which even a hypothesis could be formed. Tradition—that perishable yet ever-renewed monument of the primitive world—throws no light on the subject. It is an undoubted fact, however, that in this part of the globe thousands of our fellow beings once lived. When they came here, what their origin, their destiny, their history were, and how they perished, no one can tell. How strange it seems that nations have existed and then so completely vanished from the earth that the memory of their very names is erased; their languages are lost; their glory has vanished like a sound without an echo—though perhaps there is not one that has not left behind some tomb in memory of its passage. The most lasting monument of human labor is the one that recalls the wretchedness and nothingness of man.

Although the vast country we have been describing was inhabited by many indigenous tribes, it may justly be said that at the time of its discovery by Europeans it formed one great desert. The Indians occupied it without possessing it. It is through agricultural labor that man takes possession of the soil, and the early inhabitants of North America lived by the produce of the hunt. Their implacable prejudices, their uncontrolled passions, their vices, and still more perhaps their savage virtues, consigned them to inevitable destruction. The ruin of these nations began the day Europeans landed on their shores; it has continued ever since, and we are now witnessing its completion. They seem to have been placed by Providence amidst the riches of the New World to enjoy them for a season and then surrender them. Those coasts so admirably suited for commerce and industry; those wide and deep rivers; that inexhaustible valley of the Mississippi—the whole continent, in short—seemed prepared to be the home of a great nation, yet unborn.

In that land the great experiment was to be made by civilized man: the attempt to build society on a new foundation. It was there, for the first time, that theories until then unknown, or deemed impracticable, were to present a spectacle for which the history of the past had not prepared the world.
